visitorDetails.overview: Banks Island is an officially named island between Hecate Strait and Principe Channel in the Range 4 Coast Land District.

background.history: The BC Geographical Names record says Captain Duncan named the island in 1788 for Sir Joseph Banks. The name was adopted in 1924.

visitorDetails.overview: Bowen Island is an officially named island at the entrance to Howe Sound, west of West Vancouver.

background.history: The BC Geographical Names record says Captain Richards named the island in 1860 for Rear Admiral James Bowen. It records the Squamish name Kwílakm and notes traditional harvesting and hunting uses.
background.culturalContext: The record identifies Kwílakm as a Squamish name and describes the island as a traditional place for clam gathering, sea lion and whale hunting.

visitorDetails.overview: Calvert Island is an officially named island west of the entrance to Rivers Inlet in the Range 2 Coast Land District.
Campbell Island is an officially named island containing the community of Bella Bella, in the Range 3 Coast Land District.
Cormorant Island is an officially named island at the southeast end of Queen Charlotte Strait, between Malcolm Island and Port McNeill.

background.history: The BC Geographical Names record says Commander George T. Gordon named the island in 1846 for HMS Cormorant, a naval paddle sloop.

visitorDetails.overview: Cortes Island is an officially named island between Quadra and Redonda Islands at the north end of the Strait of Georgia.
Denman Island is an officially named island between Hornby and Vancouver Islands on the west side of the Strait of Georgia.

background.history: The BC Geographical Names record says Captain Richards named the island around 1864 for Rear Admiral Joseph Denman. It also records the K’ómoks name lháytayich and traditional use of the island for roots, shellfish, hunting, seals and cedar for canoe making.
background.culturalContext: The record attributes the name lháytayich to the K’ómoks people and describes historical resource use shared by K’ómoks First Nation.

visitorDetails.overview: Denny Island is an officially named island just east of Bella Bella, including the localities of Old Bella Bella and Shearwater.

background.history: The BC Geographical Names record says Captain Pender named the island around 1866 for Lieutenant D’Arcy Anthony Denny.

visitorDetails.overview: Flores Island is an officially named island in Clayoquot Sound, northwest of Tofino.

background.history: The BC Geographical Names record says Lieutenant Eliza named the island in 1791 for Don Manuel Antonio Flores.

visitorDetails.overview: Gabriola Island is an officially named Gulf Island just off Nanaimo on the west side of the Strait of Georgia.
Galiano Island is an officially named Gulf Island northeast of Salt Spring Island at the south end of the Strait of Georgia.

background.history: The BC Geographical Names record says Captain Richards named the island in 1859 for Spanish naval commander Dionisio Alcala Galiano. It records Kilmorey Island as a former Hudson’s Bay Company name.

visitorDetails.overview: Graham Island is the northern and largest island in the Haida Gwaii archipelago.

background.history: The BC Geographical Names record says Commander Prevost named the island in 1853 for Sir James Robert Graham.

visitorDetails.overview: Hornby Island is an officially named island on the east side of the Strait of Georgia, east of Denman Island.

background.history: The BC Geographical Names record says the island was named for Rear Admiral Phipps Hornby, commander-in-chief of the Pacific Station from 1847 to 1851.

visitorDetails.overview: Kaien Island is an officially named island between Digby Island and the Tsimpsean Peninsula in the Range 5 Coast Land District.
Lasqueti Island is an officially named island west of the south end of Texada Island.

Malcolm Island includes the seaside community of Sointula, founded by Finnish settlers in 1901. The island lies between Broughton Strait and Queen Charlotte Strait and has forest and coastal destinations.

access.directions: BC Ferries connects Sointula on Malcolm Island with Port McNeill; the tourism page describes the sailing as about 25 minutes.
access.transportNotes: The island page describes ferry access and local destinations reached by vehicle, bicycle or on foot.

trails.name: Mateoja Heritage Trail
trails.description: Begins on Third Street above Sointula and follows a route to an early 1900s homestead and Big Lake.

background.history: Sointula was established in 1901 by Finnish settlers. Its name means 'place of harmony' in Finnish.
background.culturalContext: The community page describes Finnish settlement history and the Sointula Co-operative Store Association, formed in 1909.

visitorDetails.overview: Maurelle Island is an officially named island east of the north end of Quadra Island.

background.history: The BC Geographical Names record says the name was recommended for Francisco Antonio Maurelle, a Spanish naval officer who sailed on coastal voyages in 1775 and 1779. Maurelle Island was formerly the eastern portion of Valdes Island.

visitorDetails.overview: Mayne Island is an officially named Gulf Island northeast of Salt Spring Island at the south end of the Strait of Georgia.

background.history: The BC Geographical Names record says Captain Richards named the island around 1860 for Lieutenant Richard Charles Mayne. Halliday Island was a Hudson’s Bay Company name for Mayne and Pender Islands.

visitorDetails.overview: Meares Island is an officially named island north of Tofino in Clayoquot Sound on the west side of Vancouver Island.

background.history: The BC Geographical Names record says Captain Richards named the island in 1861 for Commander John Meares.
background.culturalContext: The record also lists wančas hiłḥuuʔis as another name for the island.

visitorDetails.overview: Moresby Island is south of Graham Island and is the second largest island in the Haida Gwaii archipelago.

background.history: The BC Geographical Names record says Commander James Prevost named the island in 1853 for his father-in-law, Rear Admiral Fairfax Moresby. It also describes the island as a focus of the campaign that led to protection of much of the area as Gwaii Haanas National Park Reserve.

visitorDetails.overview: Nootka Island is on the northwest side of Nootka Sound, northwest of Tofino on the west side of Vancouver Island.
North Pender Island is an officially named Gulf Island east of Salt Spring Island at the south end of the Strait of Georgia.

background.culturalContext: The BC Geographical Names record notes the traditional SENĆOŦEN name S¸DÁYES and gives its meaning as “wind drying,” referring to drying salmon.

visitorDetails.overview: Penelakut Island is an officially named island south of Thetis Island on the east side of Stuart Channel, northeast of Chemainus.

background.history: The BC Geographical Names record says the name changed from Kuper Island to Penelakut Island in 2010 to reflect traditional usage, following a proposal from Penelakut Nation and agreement by other property owners. The traditional Halkomelem name Puneluxtth refers to a village on the island.
background.culturalContext: The record attributes the name Puneluxtth and associated account of long-term habitation to Penelakut Nation information. It gives possible translations as “log half buried in the sand” or “cedar in the mud.”

visitorDetails.overview: Pitt Island is an officially named island between Banks Island and Grenville Channel in the Range 4 Coast Land District.
Porcher Island is an officially named island off the mouth of the Skeena River, south of Prince Rupert.
Princess Royal Island is an officially named island on the east side of Hecate Strait, between Bella Bella and Kitimat.

background.history: The BC Geographical Names record says Captain Charles Duncan named the island in 1788 for his sloop Princess Royal.

visitorDetails.overview: Quadra Island is an officially named island off the east side of Vancouver Island at the north end of the Strait of Georgia.

background.history: The BC Geographical Names record says the island was named for Spanish naval officer Juan Francisco de la Bodega y Quadra. It also notes that Quadra, Sonora and Maurelle Islands were once charted together as Valdes Island before later surveys distinguished them.

visitorDetails.overview: Read Island is an officially named island between Quadra and Cortes Islands.

source.authority: Salt Spring Island Chamber of Commerce

visitorDetails.overview: Salt Spring Island is a Gulf Island between forest and coast, reached by ferry, floatplane, private boat or kayak. Visitor information describes island communities, coastal and forest walks, and local arts and food culture.

activities.name: Walking and hiking
activities.details: The visitor guide lists Duck Creek Park, Burgoyne Bay, Ruckle Park, Daffodil Point and Channel Ridge as island walking or hiking destinations.

activities.name: Cycling
activities.details: The visitor guide describes scenic island roads with hills and winding routes.

access.directions: BC Ferries serves Long Harbour from Tsawwassen, Fulford Harbour from Swartz Bay, and Vesuvius from Crofton. The page also describes floatplane, private boat and kayak access.
access.transportNotes: BC Transit operates six routes connecting Ganges, communities and the three ferry terminals; schedules are seasonal. Island roads are hilly and winding, per the visitor guide.

visitorDetails.overview: Saturna Island is an officially named Gulf Island southeast of Salt Spring Island at the south end of the Strait of Georgia.
Sonora Island is an officially named island north of Quadra Island, in front of the entrance to Bute Inlet.

background.history: The BC Geographical Names record says the island was named for the schooner Sonora, sailed by Spanish naval lieutenant Juan Francisco de la Bodega y Quadra in 1775. Sonora was formerly the northern portion of Valdes Island.

visitorDetails.overview: South Pender Island is an officially named Gulf Island east of Salt Spring Island at the south end of the Strait of Georgia.
Swindle Island is an officially named island south of Princess Royal Island.
Texada Island is an officially named island on the east side of the Strait of Georgia, south of Powell River.

background.culturalContext: The record notes that the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh name is Lháwtíkán and Spílksen.

visitorDetails.overview: Thetis Island is an officially named island west of the north end of Galiano Island.
Valdes Island is an officially named Gulf Island on the west side of the Strait of Georgia, between Galiano and Gabriola Islands.

background.history: The BC Geographical Names record says Captain Richards named Valdes Island in 1859 for Spanish naval commander Cayetano Valdés. It records the Hul’qumi’num name Láyksen and identifies the island as the traditional homeland of Lyackson First Nation. Trincomalee Island was a Hudson’s Bay Company name for Valdes Island.
background.culturalContext: The record identifies Láyksen as the Hul’qumi’num name and the island as the traditional homeland of Lyackson First Nation.

visitorDetails.overview: Vargas Island is an officially named island northwest of Tofino on the west side of Vancouver Island.

Glacier National Park has alpine peaks, deep forested valleys, old-growth cedar rainforest, alpine meadows, and railway history at Rogers Pass. The park is accessible by vehicle via the Trans-Canada Highway. Valley trails generally open around late May; higher trails may remain snow-covered into early July. Day-use areas begin opening in June and campgrounds typically in late June.

access.directions: Accessible by vehicle via the Trans-Canada Highway (Highway 1). Rogers Pass is between Golden and Revelstoke.

operations.seasons: The park is open year-round. Seasonal trail and campground openings vary.

visitorDetails.overview: Gulf Islands National Park Reserve protects island and marine habitats in the Salish Sea, where eagles and seabirds soar and seals, otters, orcas and porpoises use sheltered waters. Park areas are spread across southern Gulf Islands.

access.directions: Mayne, Saturna and Pender Islands are reached by car ferry from Swartz Bay. Sidney Spit is reached by summer passenger ferry from Sidney. Other areas are reached by kayak, powerboat or sailboat.

rules.campfires: Campfires are not permitted at backcountry campsites, including below the high-tide mark.

operations.seasons: Some park areas are open year-round, with winter access restrictions. Frontcountry camping season is May 15 to September 30; backcountry camping is year-round.

camping.summary: The reserve has two drive-in campgrounds and backcountry campgrounds on eight islands. Frontcountry campgrounds operate May 15 to September 30; backcountry campgrounds are accessible year-round but are not regularly maintained October 1 to May 14. Backcountry sites have no potable water and do not permit campfires.
camping.reservationNotes: Campsite reservations require the applicant to be at least 19; minors must be accompanied by an adult.

visitorDetails.overview: Gwaii Haanas is a remote protected area of rainforest islands, marine waters and culturally important Haida sites, co-managed by the Haida Nation and Parks Canada. Access is by sea or air; there are no roads into the area.

access.directions: There are no roads into Gwaii Haanas. Access is by boat or seaplane; a common boat route follows the inside waters of Carmichael and Dana Passages from Moresby Camp.

other.name: Self-guided trip requirements
other.details: Visitors must reserve, pay the visitor use fee and complete the online orientation before entering. Carry the booking receipt and orientation certificate; cell service is unavailable in Gwaii Haanas.

other.name: Remote travel preparedness
other.details: Visitors must be self-sufficient. No fuelling stations are available in Gwaii Haanas.

operations.seasons: Gwaii Haanas is open to visitors. Peak visitor season is June through September.
operations.notes: Weather and marine conditions affect access.

visitorDetails.overview: Kootenay National Park is a landscape of glacier-carved valleys and canyons, grasslands shaped by fire, and the historic Banff-Windermere Highway. Visitor services are available from May to mid-October.

access.directions: Highway 93 South (Banff-Windermere Highway) runs 94 km through the park. There is no public transportation, fuel station, food service, cellular or Wi-Fi service in the park.

operations.seasons: The park is open year-round. Visitor services operate May to mid-October.

visitorDetails.overview: Mount Revelstoke National Park spans rainforest to alpine meadows. The paved 26 km Meadows in the Sky Parkway climbs to the summit, with hiking trails at Balsam Lake and wildflower meadows.

access.directions: See Parks Canada directions and access information: https://parks.canada.ca/pn-np/bc/revelstoke/visit

operations.seasons: The park is open year-round; the summit parkway is a seasonal road.

visitorDetails.overview: Pacific Rim National Park Reserve protects long sandy beaches, temperate rainforest and marine landscapes in the traditional territories of Nuu-chah-nulth First Nations. Its three units are Long Beach, West Coast Trail and Broken Group Islands.

access.directions: Long Beach Unit is reached by Highway 4 from Port Alberni. The Broken Group Islands are only accessible by boat. West Coast Trail access is through Bamfield, Nitinaht Village or Port Renfrew.

operations.seasons: Long Beach Unit access is year-round. West Coast Trail and Broken Group Islands units are open to overnight visitors May 1 to September 30. Green Point Campground generally operates May to mid-October.

visitorDetails.overview: Yoho National Park lies on the western slopes of the Great Divide, where glaciers and waterfalls meet towering peaks. Highway 1 runs through the park and Field is its only community.

access.directions: Highway 1 (Trans-Canada Highway) runs 45 km through the park. It is the only major route; there is no public transportation. The Little Yoho Valley Road to Takakkaw Falls closes each winter because of avalanche hazard.

operations.seasons: The park is open year-round. Peak season is July and August; some hiking trails remain snowbound until mid-June and campgrounds generally operate May to October.

visitorDetails.overview: A boat-access only beach area with forested upland. No facilities are provided at this site. Poplar Point offers an opportunity for lakeshore camping and day-use in a wilderness marine setting. Adams Lake is noted for fishing and boating. The park protects a portion of Adams Lake beach and an upland forest of Douglas-fir, western redcedar and cottonwoods. See also Adams Lake Marine Park – Spillman Beach or Refuge Bay . Conservation The park protects a portion of Adams Lake beach and an upland forest of Douglas-fir, western redcedar and cottonwoods.

activities.name: Windsurfing
activities.details: Adams Lake can get strong winds that are great for windsurfing.

activities.name: Waterskiing
activities.details: Adams Lake has waterskiing opportunities. Adams Lake is a very large lake and it’s water conditions can change quickly. Be aware of the weather and water conditions before waterskiing. There are no motor size restrictions on Adams Lake.

activities.name: Canoeing
activities.details: There are kayak and canoe camping opportunities on Adams Lake. There are many camping opportunities that are marine access only.

activities.name: Scuba diving
activities.details: There are scuba diving opportunities in Adams Lake.

activities.name: Swimming
activities.details: There are swimming opportunities at this park. There is no roped-off swimming area at this park.

activities.name: Fishing
activities.details: Fishing is popular at Adams Lake for kokanee and rainbow trout.

activities.name: Wildlife viewing
activities.details: There are no viewing platforms but there are wildlife viewing opportunities.

activities.name: Caving
activities.details: White-Nose Syndrome White-Nose Syndrome (WNS) is a fungal disease linked to the mass die-off of hibernating bats in Eastern North America. Humans have accelerated spread by bringing contaminated clothing, gear, and equipment into caves. To learn more about White-Nose Syndrome, read the White-Nose Syndrome fact sheet [PDF] , or visit the Canadian Wildlife Health Cooperative website. Before you enter a cave, use the gear decontamination instructions .

access.directions: On the east side of Adams Lake, where Bugcamp Creek enters the lake - boat access only. The closest communities, towns and cities are Scotch Creek, Sorrento, Salmon Arm and Kamloops.

rules.pets: Pets/domestic animals must be on a leash at all times and are not allowed in beach areas or park buildings. You are responsible for their behaviour and must dispose of their excrement. Backcountry areas are not suitable for dogs or other pets due to wildlife issues and the potential for problems with bears.

operations.notes: Safety: Adams Lake is a large lake and is subject to gusts of strong wind. Note that there are few pullouts available during the high water period of May to June. Bring your own drinking water; potable water is not available in the park. Visitor Safety Information (park safety, hazards, wildlife safety information, health risks)

camping.summary:
Marine-accessible camping: Wilderness camping is allowed, but no facilities are provided. There are many camping opportunities that are marine access, only.
Wilderness camping: Wilderness camping is allowed, but no facilities are provided.

visitorDetails.overview: Refuge Bay provides one of the few secure boat landing sites on the north end of Adams Lake. The park offers an opportunity for lakeshore camping for both vehicle and boat access. Adams Lake is noted for fishing and boating. The park has limited facilities, so campers should be self-sufficient. See also Adams Lake Marine Park – Spillman Beach or Poplar Point . History Established June 2000. Conservation The park protects a small undisturbed mixed stand of cedar, spruce and hemlock as well as extensive varied aged Douglas fir and lodgepole pine forests.

activities.name: Canoeing
activities.details: There are kayak and canoe camping opportunities on Adams Lake. There are many camping opportunities that are marine access only.

activities.name: Windsurfing
activities.details: Adams Lake can get strong winds - great for windsurfing.

activities.name: Scuba diving

activities.name: Swimming
activities.details: There are swimming opportunities at this park. There is no roped-off swimming area at this park.

activities.name: Wildlife viewing
activities.details: There are no viewing platforms but there are wildlife viewing opportunities.

facilities.name: Pit or flush toilets
facilities.details: This park has one user maintained pit toilet - no flush toilets.

access.directions: Located at the north west end of Adams Lake. The closest communities, towns and cities are Scotch Creek, Chase, Vavenby, Barriere and Kamloops.

rules.pets: Pets/domestic animals must be on a leash at all times and are not allowed in beach areas or park buildings. You are responsible for their behaviour and must dispose of their excrement. Backcountry areas are not suitable for dogs or other pets due to wildlife issues and the potential for problems with bears.
rules.campfires: To preserve vegetation and ground cover, please don’t gather firewood from the area around your campsite or elsewhere in the park. Dead wood is an important habitat element for many plants and animals and it adds organic matter to the soil. You can conserve firewood and air quality by keeping your campfire small. Bring a portable stove for cooking.

camping.summary: Frontcountry camping: This park offers camping opportunities to a maximum of five camping units. Sites are primitive with no tables or metal fire rings. Due to the small scale of the camping sites and access road, camping with large recreational units is not recommended.

scope.matchedName: Adams Lake Park – Bush Creek Site

visitorDetails.overview: This pleasant beach area with a lightly forested upland is popular for fishing and boating. Adams Lake Park - Bush Creek Site has few facilities therefor visitors should be self-sufficient campers. See also Adams Lake Marine Park – Spillman Beach , or Poplar Point or Refuge Bay .

activities.name: Hiking
activities.details: For your own safety and the preservation of the park, obey posted signs and keep to designated trails. Shortcutting trails destroys plant life and soil structure.

activities.name: Canoeing
activities.details: There are opportunities for canoeing and kayaking at this park.

activities.name: Swimming
activities.details: At the campground there is a natural sand and pebble beach on Adams Lake. There is no roped off swimming area.

activities.name: Fishing
activities.details: It is popular to fish for kokanee and rainbow trout at Adams Lake. Access to the park is closed after snowfall accumulations are deep enough to make the road unsafe.

activities.name: Wildlife viewing
activities.details: There are great viewing opportunities of Adams Lake from the Adams Lake West Road.

activities.name: Cycling
activities.details: Cycling is permitted only on public and park roads. Bicycle helmets are mandatory in British Columbia. Please note that bicycles with electric assist motors (e-bikes) are not allowed on the trails within Adams Lake Park – Bush Creek Site. E-bikes are restricted to park roads and areas where motorized use is permitted. The only exception to this policy will be for authorized and identified trail maintenance bikes conducting work on behalf of BC Parks.

activities.name: Waterskiing
activities.details: Adams Lake has waterskiing opportunities. Adams Lake is a very large lake and it’s water conditions can change quickly. Be aware of the weather and water conditions before waterskiing. There are no motor size restrictions on Adams Lake.

activities.name: Windsurfing
activities.details: Adams Lake can get strong winds, which are great for windsurfing.

activities.name: Scuba diving
activities.details: There are scuba diving opportunities in Adams Lake.

facilities.name: Pit or flush toilets
facilities.details: This park only has pit toilets, no flush toilets.

facilities.name: Boat launch
facilities.details: There is an undeveloped gravel boat launch. The small parking area for vehicles and boat trailers is at the bottom of the entrance road, before the camping area. Please check with the park operator before parking any vehicles or trailers in the parking area. It is prohibited to park vehicles on any roadways within the park.

access.directions: The park is on the southwestern shores of Adams Lake. It is located 15 km from Highway 1 at Squilax, east of Kamloops, 30 km north of Chase. Take the Holding/Adams Lake West Road off the Squilax-Anglemont Road. The closest communities are Scotch Creek, Sorrento, Salmon Arm, Kamloops and Chase.

rules.pets: Pets and domestic animals must be on a leash at all times and are not allowed in beach areas. You are responsible for their behaviour and must dispose of their excrement.
rules.cycling: Cycling is permitted only on public and park roads. Bicycle helmets are mandatory in British Columbia. Please note that bicycles with electric assist motors (e-bikes) are not allowed on the trails within Adams Lake Park – Bush Creek Site. E-bikes are restricted to park roads and areas where motorized use is permitted. The only exception to this policy will be for authorized and identified trail maintenance bikes conducting work on behalf of BC Parks.
rules.campfires: Campfires are allowed and campfire rings are provided at each campsite. We encourage visitors to conserve wood and protect the environment by minimizing the use of fire and using campstoves instead. The park operator does not provide firewood in this park. However, you are welcome to bring your own firewood as long as it meets current campfire restrictions of 0.5 m by 0.5 m in size. To preserve vegetation and ground cover, please don’t gather firewood from the area around your campsite or elsewhere in the park (this is a ticketable offence under the Park Act ). Dead wood is an important habitat element for many plants and animals and it adds organic matter to the soil.

operations.notes:
Safety: Adams is a large lake, and subject to gusts of strong wind. Note that there are few pullouts available during the high water of May and June. Bring your own water, as potable water is not available in the park. Visitors must stay on the trails and within the viewing area. Rocks and river edges can be extremely slippery.
Notes: The nearest telephone is located at Adams Lake Store, approximately 5 km from the park. Consumption of alcohol is prohibited in provincial parks, except within your campsite. Adams Lake West Forest Service Road frequently has heavy logging truck traffic. Use caution on this road and yield to logging trucks. Please help to prevent the spread of Eurasian Water Milfoil by removing all weeds from your boat and motor before launching and after removing from the lake. Please be advised that overnight parking for boat launch use is not permitted. Only vehicles registered for overnight camping will be permitted. All other vehicles will be towed at owners expense.
A park gate is listed for this park; opening times and dates vary.

camping.summary: Frontcountry camping: This park offers vehicle-accessible campsites on a first come, first served basis. You can self-register by choosing a site and depositing payment at the pay station. Campsite reservations are not accepted. The campsites are suitable for campers and small trailers only. There are no pull-through campsites. All sites are shaded and very rustic, with fire rings. There is no gatehouse at this park. There is limited parking for extra vehicles. The park may be accessible earlier and later depending on weather and snow-load. The gates are closed in the off-season and camping is not permitted.
camping.reservationNotes: BC Parks lists first-come, first-served camping at this park. Check the official page for current reservation rules.

background.history: The area was established for recreational use in 1988. It obtained park designation in 1997 as a result of the Kamloops Land and Resource Management Plan.
background.conservation: The park protects beaches and shoreline on Adams Lake as well as mixed forests of aspen, birch, willow, Douglas fir and cedar.
background.culturalContext: There are a number of known archaeological sites at this park.

visitorDetails.overview: Akamina Kishinena Park is located in the southeast corner of the province. Along with Waterton Lakes National Park and US Glacier National Park, this wilderness area preserves the narrowest point of the Rocky Mountains. High spacious alpine ridges, deep secluded valleys and windswept passes provide habitat and connectivity to the last self-sustaining grizzly bear population in the United States. Exposed alpine ridges, southern latitude and southern exposure provide winter range for goats and big horn sheep. The trails and passes of the Akamina-Kishinena used today to cross the axis of the continent, were established and used for many years by the early people’s and wildlife travelling between the Flathead Basin and the abundant Great Plains.

activities.name: Fishing
activities.details: Anglers fish for rainbow trout in Forum and Wall Lakes. BC fishing licenses are no longer available in Waterton. Refer to the ministry website for the nearest vendor .

activities.name: Hiking
activities.details: The park offers hiking opportunities for beginners as well as experienced backcountry travellers: Akamina Pass: This old road built in the 1920s transects the park from Akamina Pass through the Kishinena Creeks to eventually reach the Flathead River valley. Cyclists use this route for day excursions from Waterton Lakes. Forum Lake and Falls: From the Ranger Station, it is 200 m to the falls and 2 km to the lake. The hike to Forum Lake takes about 45 minutes with a climb of 200 m. Wall Lake: From the Akamina Road (200 m) from the Ranger Station it is 2 km to Wall Lake, 50 m elevation gain. For your own safety and preservation of the park, obey posted signs and keep to designated trails. Shortcutting trails destroys plant life and soil structure. Only experienced hikers with orienteering experience should consider following routes and unmarked trails in the park. Akamina-Kishinena Park trail conditions report [PDF]

activities.name: Cycling
activities.details: Mountain biking is permitted on designated trails only. Bicycle helmets are mandatory in British Columbia. For details on e-biking within Akamina-Kishinena Park, see the e-biking section.

activities.name: Horseback riding
activities.details: If planning to horseback ride in the park, we recommend you read the Akamina Kishinena Horse Use Policy [PDF] . As horseback riders are required to obtain and carry with them a letter of permission from BC Parks please use our online form to generate and print your letter of permission, no less than seven days before entering the park. More specific information on using horses in the park can be obtained by contacting the Kootenay BC Parks office at 250-489-8540 . There is no horse use allowed to Forum Lake, and riders travelling to Wall Lake must use the horse trail.

activities.name: Hunting
activities.details: The discharge and carrying of firearms is permitted in this park for the purposes of hunting during open season. Please consult the BC Government Hunting and Trapping Regulations Synopsis for more information. Contact BC Parks at parkinfo@gov.bc.ca with any specific questions. Horse-assisted hunting trips are allowed during open seasons, but only with a Letter of Permission .

activities.name: E-Biking
activities.details: Please note that bicycles with electric assist motors (e-bikes) are permitted on signed or designated trails within Akamina-Kishinena Park, provided they meet the definitions and criteria for e-bike use as outlined in the BC Parks cycling guidelines .

activities.name: Winter recreation
activities.details: There are opportunities for ice fishing in the park.

facilities.name: Pit or flush toilets
facilities.details: This park only has pit toilets, no flush toilets.

access.directions: From Highway 3, turn south at Pincher Creek onto Highway 6. From the park gate, access the Cameron Lake park road to reach the Akamina Pass trailhead (16 km). A 30 minute, 1.5 km uphill walk reaches the boundary between Alberta and BC and the eastern border of Akamina-Kishinena Park. The closest communities are Waterton Lakes National Park community and Sparwood. It is 48 km to Waterton Lakes National Park.

rules.pets: Pets and domestic animals must be on a leash at all times and are not allowed in beach areas or park buildings. You are responsible for their behaviour and must dispose of their excrement. Dogs in backcountry parks must be on a leash at all times. Backcountry areas are not suitable for dogs or other pets due to the potential for problems with bears and other wildlife.
rules.cycling: Mountain biking is permitted on designated trails only. Bicycle helmets are mandatory in British Columbia. For details on e-biking within Akamina-Kishinena Park, see the e-biking section.
rules.campfires: Fires in the developed area of the park are restricted to a communal fire ring in the Akamina Creek campground. Be prepared by bringing a portable stove for cooking. Fires in the backcountry areas must be kept small, contained and a source of water to extinguish the fire must be readily available. To preserve vegetation and ground cover, please don’t gather firewood from the area around your campsite when staying in the developed area of the park. Dead wood is an important habitat element for many plants and animals and it adds organic matter to the soil. You can conserve firewood and air quality by keeping your campfire small.

operations.notes: Safety: Akamina-Kishinena Park trail conditions report [PDF] The park is a wilderness area without supplies or equipment of any kind. All arrangements for supplies and transportation must be made in advance. Weather conditions can change suddenly, and lightning storms with hail and snow are common in summer. Wear strong, water-proofed, lug-soled boots. Carry a day-pack with rain gear, extra clothing, and food. For overnight trips, a sleeping bag, ground pad, water-proof tent or bivouac bag, and light-weight stove are essential. Bring your own drinking water, as potable water is not available in the park. To ensure that water from streams is safe to drink, it must be boiled for at least five minutes or treated or filtered. Only experienced climbers, practiced in crevasse rescue and properly roped, should venture onto snowfields. Loaded logging trucks and other industrial traffic may be encountered while accessing this park from British Columbia. Drive with extreme caution, and for your safety, always yield to industrial traffic. Public communications are not available at this park. Learn more about backcountry safety in our backcountry guide .

camping.summary:
Backcountry camping: A backcountry campground with ten wilderness sawdust tent pads, outhouse, and food cache is provided at Akamina Creek. This campground is located just off the main trail 0.9 km from Akamina Pass and 2.4 km from the Akamina Pass Trailhead. Register a trip itinerary with friends and check in and check out. Winter camping is available year-round at Akamina Creek sites. Although this does not reserve a campsite, it provides the convenience of prepaying for your trip and not having to carry cash.
Winter camping: A backcountry campground with ten wilderness sawdust tent pads, outhouse and food cache is provided at Akamina Creek. This campground is located just off the main trail 0.9km from Akamina Pass and 2.4 km from the Akamina Pass Trailhead. Register a trip itinerary with friends and check in and check out. Winter camping is available year-round at Akamina Creek sites. Although this does not reserve a campsite, it provides the convenience of prepaying for your trip and not having to carry cash.

BC Parks lists first-come, first-served camping at this park. Check the official page for current reservation rules.

background.history: This area is of great interest to geologists. The formations of the Akamina-Kishinena are made of the oldest exposed rock in the Canadian Rockies. The shore of Forum Lake is paved with colourful limestone estimated to be 1.3 billion years old. Remnants of oil rigs first hauled into camps on winter trails in 1905 are still visible. No economically significant wells were drilled, nor did any of the mining claims staked in the 1950s and 1960s prove viable. Other resources were explored by trappers and hunters, and a small saw mill operated at Akamina Creek. The spectacular southeast corner of the province was recommended for preservation as early as 1917. In 1995, Akamina-Kishinena became a class A provincial park.
background.conservation: Weather fronts from the Pacific meet arctic and prairie influences to intermingle at this axis. They create a diversity of plant species, including rare species like the yellow monkey flower and pigmy poppy, that are found nowhere else in British Columbia.
background.culturalContext: Cairns trace the paths of the Ktunaxa Indigenous people. They travelled through South Kootenay Pass to reach the plains for trading and buffalo hunting.

visitorDetails.overview: Alexandra Bridge Park is a small park centred around the site of the original Cariboo Wagon Road bridge over the Fraser River. It provides both a rest stop and picnic facilities for travelers. This site has been a natural stop-over and crossing of the Fraser River since the area was first populated. Because of its small size there are limited recreational opportunities within this park.

activities.name: Cycling
activities.details: Bicycles must keep to roadways. Bicycle helmets are mandatory in British Columbia. Please note that bicycles with electric assist motors (e-bikes) are not allowed on the trails within Alexandra Bridge Park. E-bikes are restricted to park roads and areas where motorized use is permitted. The only exception to this policy will be for authorized and identified trail maintenance bikes conducting work on behalf of BC Parks.

facilities.name: Picnic areas
facilities.details: Located adjacent to Highway 1, this day-use site offers six picnic tables and three pit toilets in a coastal forest setting. There are small grassy areas and most picnic sites are shaded throughout the day. There are two paved parking areas. The day-use area is open from May 15 to October 15.

facilities.name: Pit or flush toilets
facilities.details: This park has three pit toilets, no flush toilets. One pit toilet in the park is wheelchair-accessible.

access.directions: Alexandra Bridge Park is situated adjacent to the Fraser River approximately 2 km north of Spuzzum and 40 km north of Hope. Access is available from both north and south bound lanes off the Trans Canada Highway.

rules.pets: Pets and domestic animals must be on a leash at all times and are not allowed in beach areas or park buildings.
rules.cycling: Bicycles must keep to roadways. Bicycle helmets are mandatory in British Columbia. Please note that bicycles with electric assist motors (e-bikes) are not allowed on the trails within Alexandra Bridge Park. E-bikes are restricted to park roads and areas where motorized use is permitted. The only exception to this policy will be for authorized and identified trail maintenance bikes conducting work on behalf of BC Parks.

accessibility.summary: Accessibility information is available for this park. https://accessibility.bcparks.ca/parks/#330-410

operations.notes:
Notes: The bridge itself is not in the park. It is maintained by the Ministry of Transportation and Infrastructure.
A park gate is listed for this park; opening times and dates vary.

background.history: Alexandra Bridge Park was established in 1984 because of its inherent natural, historical and recreational attributes. The area has been used and inhabited by First Nations for over 9,500 years. The first European visit did not occur until Simon Fraser’s expedition passed through the region in 1808. The first permanent trail, the Anderson Brigade trail, was then established in 1848 and subsequently, the original bridge was constructed in 1861 by Joseph W. Trutch and named after Princess Alexandra of Wales. To recover the $45,000 construction cost for the 90 metre bridge, a toll of $7.40 per ton was charged. Today a second bridge, built in 1926, sits on the site of the original which was dismantled in 1912.
background.conservation: The landscape is characterized by major low elevation valleys and the densely forested mountain slopes of a wet climate. Alexandra Bridge Park sits at the eastern border of the Western Hemlock forest subzone. As such, it contains many western hemlock, western red cedar and Douglas-fir. Rising steeply on the east bank of the Fraser River, the site contains two well defined glaciofluvial benches.
background.culturalContext: Alexandra Bridge Park and other areas along the Fraser River were traditional fishing grounds for the Halkomelum (Stalo) and Lower Thompson First Nations. The local native bands still use this area for traditional fishing.
background.wildlife: The Fraser River is the largest fish producing water course in the province. Because of this, millions of spring, coho, chum, pink and sockeye salmon pass through the park on their way to spawning grounds every year.

visitorDetails.overview: Alice Lake is a popular family park surrounded by towering mountains, dense forests, and grassy areas. Four freshwater lakes dominate the landscape, making this a great park for swimming and fishing. The trail around Alice Lake is a popular spot for evening strolls while more adventurous hikers, will enjoy the Four Lakes Trail . The DeBeck’s Hill Trail , meanwhile, offers excellent views of the Squamish River and the Tantalus Range.

activities.name: Hiking
activities.details: Trails in this park include The Four Lakes Trail, Mike’s Loop, Stump Lake Loop Trail, Alice Lake Loop Trail, Swamp Lantern Interpretive Loop Trail, Bob MacIntosh Memorial Trail, Jacks Trail, DeBeck’s Hill Trail, Tracks from Hell Trail, and trails to the Lower Alice Ridge. The last five trails head out of the park. For your own safety and the preservation of the park, obey posted signs and keep to designated trails. Taking shortcuts destroys plant life and soil structure. For more information see Alice Lake Park: Hiking .

activities.name: Canoeing
activities.details: Canoes and kayaks are allowed on the lake. There are paddle sport services available during the summer months. Motorized boats are not permitted.

activities.name: Fishing
activities.details: Fishing opportunities are available in all four lakes, for rainbow trout, Dolly Varden, and some cutthroat. Fishing is prohibited in the designated swim areas as marked by the swim lines.

activities.name: Swimming
activities.details: There are two sandy beach areas with change houses. The water is usually warm in the summer months. Swimming areas are marked by floats and a floating dock is available at South Beach, a short walk from the campground.

activities.name: Interpretive programs
activities.details: Find fun summer outdoor learning experiences with Discover Parks Ambassadors here all summer long. For specific dates, along with many more seasonal and year-round activities, visit discoverparks.ca . The Freshwater Fisheries Society has a fun, hands-on, Learn to Fish Program that teaches basic angling skills to youth under 16 years of age. Ask the park operator for information.

activities.name: Cycling
activities.details: Mountain biking is permitted on certain trails and park roadways. See the park map [PDF] for details. Refer to guidebooks for information about the extensive mountain bike trails in the Squamish area. The section of Four Lakes Trail between Edith Lake and Alice Lake (South Beach) and the trail around Alice Lake are permanently closed to cycling. The remainder of Four Lakes Trail is closed to cycling between May 1 and September 15. For details on e-biking within Alice Lake Park, see the e-biking section.

activities.name: E-Biking
activities.details: Bicycles with electric assist motors (e-bikes) are permitted on signed or designated trails within Alice Lake Park, provided they meet the definitions and criteria outlined in our e-bike rules .

facilities.name: Picnic areas
facilities.details: Alice Lake Park has a day-use and picnicking area with picnic tables and a parking lot. There are no covered shelters. There are two sandy beaches and a grassy area nearby. The main toilet building includes changing facilities. There are no fire rings or fires permitted in the day-use area. During the main camping season, the day-use area closes at 11pm. During the off-season, if the gate is locked, the day-use area can still be accessed by foot.

facilities.name: Pit or flush toilets
facilities.details: Flush toilets are available in the campground and the day-use area. Pit toilets are provided throughout the park.

facilities.name: Drinking water
facilities.details: There are water taps in the campground. Water taps and water fountains are available in the day-use area. Taps are shut off during the off-season.

facilities.name: Playground
facilities.details: Alice Lake Park includes a playground area with a slide and other equipment within view of the lake, less than five minutes walk from the day-use parking lot.

facilities.name: Electrical hook-ups
facilities.details: Alice Lake Park now offers 55 vehicle-accessible campsites and one group camping area with electrical hook-ups. Each site provides 30-amp service with one standard RV receptacle (NEMA TT-30) and one 15-amp standard household receptacle (NEMA 5).

facilities.name: Showers
facilities.details: Shower facilities are available for registered guests. There are two shower buildings in the campground, which provide hot water and electrical outlets for hairdryers and razors.

facilities.name: Sani-station
facilities.details: A sani-station is available during the collecting season. The station is closed during the winter.

access.directions: Alice Lake Park is situated off Highway 99, approximately 13km north of Squamish and 71km north of the Lions Gate Bridge in North Vancouver.

rules.pets: Domestic animals are allowed in the campground but not at the day-use area, picnic areas, beaches, or park buildings. Dogs must be on a leash at all times. Owners are responsible for their dogs' behaviour and must dispose of excrement. Backcountry areas are not suitable for pets due to the presence of bears and other wildlife.
rules.campfires: While campfires are allowed and campfire rings are provided at each campsite, we encourage visitors to conserve wood and protect the environment by minimizing the use of fire and using camping stoves instead. Firewood can be purchased in the park or you may bring your own wood. To preserve vegetation and ground cover, please do not gather firewood from the area around your campsite or elsewhere in the park (this is a ticketable offence under the Park Act). Dead wood is an important habitat element for many plants and animals and it adds organic matter to the soil.

accessibility.summary: With the exception of Four Lakes, trails in and around the day-use area are wheelchair-accessible. There are wheelchair-accessible picnic tables, and campsites 17 and 18 are also wheelchair-accessible. See more accessibility information for this park . https://accessibility.bcparks.ca/parks/#90-411

operations.notes:
You are strongly advised to make a reservation well in advance of any stay at this park planned for July, August, or September. The park is usually full even on weekdays, with little turnover of campsites in the morning. On some particularly warm weekends, the parking lots may fill up and additional visitors will not be able to drive into the park. The park has access to many mountain bike trails outside of the park. Please obey all signs while riding. Dogs must be leashed at all times and they are not allowed on the Alice Lake Trail, beaches, the playground, or in picnic areas. Quiet hours are from 10pm to 7am. Music, generators, and other sources of noise must be shut off completely between these hours. Generator use is only allowed from 9am to 11am and from 6pm to 8pm. View the generator policy . There are 55 vehicle-accessible campsites and one group camping area with electrical hook-ups . The closest store is located six kilometres away in Brackendale.
A park gate is listed for this park; opening times and dates vary.

camping.summary:
RV-accessible camping
Frontcountry camping: Campsite reservations are accepted at this park, and first come, first served sites are available until early spring, at which time all sites become reservable. When reservations are not available, all campsites are available on a first come, first served basis. All reservations must be made through the BC Parks reservation service . Campsites This park offers 96 vehicle-accessible campsites. Most of these sites can accommodate a large camper with trailer. There are also a few medium-sized sites and a couple of small sites. There are 11 double sites. The campground is set in forest cover and the sites are somewhat shaded. Sites are not on the lakeshore but are set back in the forest. Vehicles Parking on road edges is prohibited. Check-in Check-in for reservation holders is available starting at 1pm on the day of your arrival. Check out time for all reservations is 11am. Check in at the gatehouse when you arrive. During posted operating hours, staff are available to check you in. If you have a reservation, you will be directed to your reserved site. If you do not have a reservation, any site that is not already reserved is available on a first come, first served basis, and you can register and pay for your site at the gatehouse. If there are no staff available to direct you to an open site and take payment, then please check online for availability and use the online portals to reserve. You can then proceed to your site. Park Operators will be around each morning to check in on new and unpaid customers.
Walk-in camping: There are 12 walk-in (or cycle-in) campsites available at this park. Parking is very close to the walk-in sites. The walk-in campsite area has some sites that are close together, which is ideal for families or larger groups. There are food storage lockers available near the middle of the walk-in site section. Plan to pack out what you pack in. Please be bear aware and for further information read more about wildlife safety .
Group camping: Group camping reservations are accepted at this park. There are two group campsites available at this park. The sites can hold groups of 15 to 40 people. Each groupsite has tarp posts and a central fire ring. Check-in is at 1pm and check-out is at 11am. This gives the park operator time to clean the site before the next group arrives.

background.history: Alice Lake, was named for the wife of Charles Rose, who settled in the district in about 1888. It was a popular recreation spot for local residents even before the park was established in 1956.
background.wildlife: Small mammals, such as squirrels, chipmunks, and raccoons, and birds, such as stellar’s jays, crows, and osprey, can often be seen.

visitorDetails.overview: Allison Harbour Marine Park is located mid-way along the southern shore of Allison Harbour, with three pocket beaches and two creeks running through the park. The park protects important habitat for resident gray whales during the summer and second growth forest on the upland. Allison Harbour is a protected, short inlet comprised of small coves with tidal flats at the head. This is a protected transitional stop for boaters and is used as a safe anchorage from frequent southeasterly winds. The harbour is the last all-weather anchorage for boaters travelling north around Cape Caution. It is an important addition to the network of boat havens along the British Columbia coast.

Off the beaten track, you’ll find tree-bordered Allison Lake. This is a desirable spot for swimmers and those who love to fish. The park is known for its spectacular stands of aspen that burst into golden colours in the fall. Allison Lake Park is a great overnight spot when travelling between Merritt and Princeton.

activities.name: Canoeing
activities.details: The relatively small size of Allison Lake allows for safe, enjoyable paddling, canoeing and kayaking. There are no rentals in or near the park.

activities.name: Fishing
activities.details: Allison Lake is stocked with 15,000 blackwater rainbow trout raised at the Summerland trout hatchery. There are no special restrictions on the lake.

activities.name: Swimming
activities.details: Swimming opportunities are available at the park.

activities.name: Cycling
activities.details: Bicycles must keep to roadways. Bicycle helmets are mandatory in British Columbia. Please note that bicycles with electric assist motors (e-bikes) are not allowed on the trails within Allison Lake Park. E-bikes are restricted to park roads and areas where motorized use is permitted. The only exception to this policy will be for authorized and identified trail maintenance bikes conducting work on behalf of BC Parks.

activities.name: Waterskiing
activities.details: There is potential for waterskiing on Allison Lake.

facilities.name: Pit or flush toilets
facilities.details: This park only has pit toilets, no flush toilets. There are two pit toilets in the campground and two in the day-use area.

facilities.name: Drinking water
facilities.details: Two cold water taps are located in the campground. Taps are shut off during the off-season. Please review the know before you go section for any boil water notices.

facilities.name: Picnic areas
facilities.details: The day-use area is found on the southern shore of Allison Lake, across Highway 5A from the campground. There are 10 tables spread out on the non-irrigated lawns. Two pit toilets and one tap are found there. The beach is fine white sand and varies in size with the fluctuating lake levels. When water levels are low, motor vehicles are prohibited from driving on the exposed beach.

access.directions: This park is located 28 km north of Princeton, along Highway 5A. The closest community is Princeton.

rules.pets: Pets and domestic animals must be on a leash at all times and are not allowed in beach areas or park buildings. You are responsible for their behaviour and must dispose of their excrement. Backcountry areas are not suitable for dogs or other pets due to wildlife issues and the potential for problems with bears.
rules.cycling: Bicycles must keep to roadways. Bicycle helmets are mandatory in British Columbia. Please note that bicycles with electric assist motors (e-bikes) are not allowed on the trails within Allison Lake Park. E-bikes are restricted to park roads and areas where motorized use is permitted. The only exception to this policy will be for authorized and identified trail maintenance bikes conducting work on behalf of BC Parks.
rules.campfires: Campfires are allowed and campfire rings are provided at each campsite. We encourage visitors to conserve wood and protect the environment by minimizing the use of fire and using campstoves instead. Firewood can be purchased in the park or you may bring your own wood. To preserve vegetation and ground cover, please don’t gather firewood from the area around your campsite or elsewhere in the park (this is a ticketable offence under the Park Act ). Dead wood is an important habitat element for many plants and animals and it adds organic matter to the soil.

camping.summary: Frontcountry camping: This park has gravel sites, one of which is a double. There are no pull-through sites or tent pads. The sites are shaded by mature Douglas fir trees and are available on a first come, first served basis. A self-registration vault is present for payment when staff are not available. Reservations are accepted for sites 12 to 22 and the rest are available on a first come, first served basis. The closest store is in Princeton, 28 km south of the campground, and there is no phone in the park.
camping.reservationNotes:
Campsite reservations are accepted for sites 12 to 22 and the rest are available on a first come, first served basis. For parks that accept reservations, all vehicle-accessible campsites (with the exception of group sites) must be reserved through the BC Parks reservations system .

visitorDetails.overview: Ancient Forest/Chun T’oh Whudujut Park is quickly becoming one of the “must do” parks to see and hike in British Columbia. Nestled in the traditional territory of the Lheidli T’enneh, the park protects a portion of one of the only inland temperate rainforest in the world. Hiking the Ancient Forest trail will bring you past thousand year old western redcedars and a rich biodiversity of plants, mosses, lichens and fungi. The 450 metre long universal access boardwalk provides the opportunity for people with all abilities to experience this majestic area. Another 2.3 km of boardwalk provides access to magnificent “Big” Tree, Tree Beard, Radies Tree and a beautiful cascading waterfall.

activities.name: Hunting
activities.details: The discharge and carrying of firearms is permitted in this park for the purposes of hunting during open season. Please consult the BC Government Hunting and Trapping Regulations Synopsis for more information. Contact BC Parks at parkinfo@gov.bc.ca with any specific questions. This protected area is partially open to hunting. Highway set back closures are in effect as well as 400 metres from a park road.

activities.name: Hiking
activities.details: For your own safety and the preservation of the park, obey posted signs and keep to designated trails. Shortcutting trails destroys plant life and soil structure. Trail Information The Universal Access Trail is approximately 450 metres long (one way). The boardwalk will enable visitors in wheelchairs, those with other mobility or mental health challenges, and everyone else to experience the only inland temperate rainforest in the world that is so far from the ocean. Ancient Forest Boardwalk Trail is 2.3 km long and provides users with a close look at the unique inland temperate rainforest of British Columbia. Driscoll Ridge Trail is a strenuous trail 15.5 km long loop which brings you to the ridge line on the south side of the park. This trail should only be attempted by experienced, well prepared hikers, in good physical condition.

activities.name: Winter recreation
activities.details: Snowshoeing on the Ancient Forest Boardwalk Trail is a great way to see this site in the winter. Limited winter parking is available.

facilities.name: Pit or flush toilets
facilities.details: This park has universal access pit toilets. No flush toilets are available.

facilities.name: Picnic areas
facilities.details: This park has a day-use and picnic area.

access.directions: This park and associated hiking trails are located midway between Prince George and McBride on Highway 16. It is about 115 km east of PG on Highway 16 and 103 km west of McBride. The nearest cities are Prince George and McBride.
