rules.campfires: While fires are allowed, we encourage visitors to conserve the environment by minimizing the use of fire and using stoves instead. If you must use a campfire, please practice “ Leave No Trace ” camping ethics.

operations.notes: Notes: This park contains few developed facilities. There are a few wooden tent pads at the south end of the lake, as well as a composting toilet and shelter which were installed by the Namgis First Nation. This park is a wilderness area that is not regularly serviced or patrolled. Please practice Leave No Trace camping and day-use in the area. The nearest phone, store, and tourist information centre is located in the town of Zeballos.

camping.summary:
Winter camping: Woss Lake Park is open year-round.
Wilderness camping: There are no designated campsites at this park. There are no facilities but camping is allowed in all areas.

background.history: Woss Lake Park was created in 1995 as part of the Vancouver Island Land-Use Plan.
background.conservation: Woss Lake Park is a very steep, forested, seldom visited wilderness area. The park contains Roosevelt elk populations, a salmon fishery and potentially, habitat for the endangered Vancouver Island marmot. The park also contains a nameless, intact secondary watershed of 1,600 hectares that drains into the head of Woss Lake. This unnamed drainage contains valuable Chinook salmon and steelhead spawning habitat and a sensitive delta area with a variety of rare plant species. It also protects representative old-growth forest landscapes, a complete watershed of a major tributary at the south end of Woss Lake, and is dominated by Rugged Mountain and the glaciers and snowfields of its north facing slopes. The pristine old growth forested slopes above Woss Lake and the scenery offered by Rugged Mountain and its glaciers, the largest on Vancouver Island, are of provincial significance.
background.culturalContext: Woss Lake Park is within the traditional territory of the Namgis First Nation. The park contains a portion of a First Nations traditional cross-island trade route known as the Grease Trail, which made its way over the Tahsis divide. Culturally modified trees (CMTs) have been identified in the park.

visitorDetails.overview: The park protects a series of dry meadows at the top of a basalt cliff formation and the wetter meadows at its base, along with the interior Douglas fir forest. The dry, seasonally-wet, diverse meadows are extremely fragile. Five red-listed and blue-listed vascular plants are known to occur including red-listed Obscure Cryptantha and Needleleaved Navarretia as well as blue-listed Northern Linanthus, False-mermaid and Awned Cyperus squarrosus. Secondarily, the park provides low-impact recreational opportunities and contains part of the regionally-significant 55 km long High Rim Trail.

activities.name: Hiking
activities.details: There are several well-defined hiking trails in this park. For your own safety and preservation of the park, obey posted signs and keep to designated trails. Shortcutting trails destroys plant life and soil structure.

activities.name: Horseback riding
activities.details: The High Rim Trail through the park is open to horses. Please stay on designated trails.

activities.name: Climbing
activities.details: The basalt columns on the south west side of the cliff offer mountaineering opportunities for experienced climbers.

activities.name: Hunting
activities.details: The discharge and carrying of firearms is permitted in this park for the purposes of hunting during open season. Please consult the BC Government Hunting and Trapping Regulations Synopsis for more information. Contact BC Parks at parkinfo@gov.bc.ca with any specific questions.

access.directions: The approach trail is located just north-east of Winfield, at the south-west end of Long Mountain, south of Vernon. The park is accessed via the Beaver Main Forest Service Road. From Highway 97 follow Beaver Lake Road for about 12 km to the High Rim trail head. Hike north about one hour to the park.

operations.notes: Notes: Motorized vehicles are not permitted in the park. Campfires are not permitted. National Topographic Series Maps Sheet 082L/03 (Oyama) at a scale of 1:50,000 cover the area.

background.conservation: The park protects representations of the Biogeoclimatic Zones interior cedar-hemlock and interior Douglas fir. Contributions represent two percent of the total of these representations in the overall protected area system. Wild Flowers: June 2007: Northern sanicle, pygmy bitterroot. May 2005: Lupin, wild strawberry, heart-leaved arnica, small-flowered blue-eyed Mary, upland larkspur, early blue violet, annual hawksbeard, Saskatoon, low pussytoes, alpine paint brush, blue clematis, few flowered shooting star, old man’s whiskers, round-leaved alumroot, meadow death camus, fairy slipper, false Solomon’s seal, kinnikinnick, fern-leaved desert-parsley, crane’s bill, shrubby penstemon, yarrow, common dandelion. September 2004: Flowering thistle.

visitorDetails.overview: Located along Highway 3/95, 70km south of Cranbrook and 14.5km north of the US and Canadian borders at Kingsgate, Yahk Park is a traveller’s rest place. Near the Moyie River in a quiet well spaced forest this 26 site campground and day-use area is a great introduction to BC Park visitor facilities. Yahk Park was established in 1956 to provide camping and picnicking opportunities for the travelling public. As well it conserves a short scenic section of the Moyie River. The adjacent town of Yahk has services and tourist supplies. The area was once a major supplier of railroad ties for the Canadian Pacific Railway.

activities.name: Fishing
activities.details: Locals fish for trout in the Moyie River.

activities.name: Canoeing
activities.details: There are opportunities for canoeing or kayaking in this park.

activities.name: Cycling
activities.details: Bicycles must keep to roadways. Bicycle helmets are mandatory in British Columbia. Please note that bicycles with electric assist motors (e-bikes) are not allowed on the trails within Yahk Park. E-bikes are restricted to park roads and areas where motorized use is permitted. The only exception to this policy will be for authorized and identified trail maintenance bikes conducting work on behalf of BC Parks.

activities.name: Kayaking
activities.details: There are opportunities for canoeing or kayaking in this park.

facilities.name: Picnic areas
facilities.details: This park has a day-use and picnic area with tables near the river.

facilities.name: Pit or flush toilets
facilities.details: The park has four pit toilets, no flush toilets.

facilities.name: Drinking water
facilities.details: Three cold water taps are located throughout the park. Taps are shut off during the off-season.

access.directions: Yahk Park is located along Highway 3/95, 70km south of Cranbrook, 14.5km north of the U.S. and Canadian borders at Kingsgate. This park is found on the south edge of the small community of Yahk.

rules.pets: Pets and domestic animals must be on a leash at all times and are not allowed in beach areas or park buildings. You are responsible for their behaviour and must dispose of their excrement. Backcountry areas are not suitable for dogs or other pets due to wildlife issues and the potential for problems with bears.
rules.cycling: Bicycles must keep to roadways. Bicycle helmets are mandatory in British Columbia. Please note that bicycles with electric assist motors (e-bikes) are not allowed on the trails within Yahk Park. E-bikes are restricted to park roads and areas where motorized use is permitted. The only exception to this policy will be for authorized and identified trail maintenance bikes conducting work on behalf of BC Parks.
rules.campfires: While campfires are allowed and campfire rings are provided at each campsite, we encourage visitors to conserve wood and protect the environment by minimizing the use of fire and using campstoves instead. Firewood can be purchased in the park or you may bring your own wood. To preserve vegetation and ground cover, please don’t gather firewood from the area around your campsite or elsewhere in the park (this is a ticketable offence under the Park Act ). Dead wood is an important habitat element for many plants and animals and it adds organic matter to the soil.

accessibility.summary: Accessibility information is available for this park. https://accessibility.bcparks.ca/parks/#79-769

operations.notes:
Safety: The Moyie River is fast moving, especially during spring runoff. Visitors should use caution when near the banks of the river.
A park gate is listed for this park; opening times and dates vary.

camping.summary: Frontcountry camping: The park offers 26 vehicle-accessible campsites. Campsite reservations are accepted and first come, first served sites are available. For tenters, four of these campsites (sites 3, 6, 15, 24) have sand filled tent pads and function on a first come, first served basis. There is a information shelter at the entrance to this park.
camping.reservationNotes:
Frontcountry Camping Reservations Campsite reservations are accepted at this park. All drive-in and walk-in campsites are reservable during peak season. There are no first come, first served sites. Group Camping Reservations Group campsite reservations are accepted at this park (minimum 15 adults) year-round. The picnic and day-use area is available on a first come, first served basis only and is not reservable at this park. All campsite and group site reservations must be made the BC Parks reservations system .
BC Parks lists first-come, first-served camping at this park. Check the official page for current reservation rules.

visitorDetails.overview: Yalakom Park provides extensive representation of the Camelsfoot Range. The park protects the whole of the undeveloped basin of Yalakom Creek and much of Nine Mile Ridge. It has a landscape of old-growth, dry and riparian forest as well as high elevation aspen stands, alpine grasslands and krumholz forest. Thick metamorphosed sedimentary rocks forming scarp and dipslope topography. Yalakom also contains multiple California bighorn sheep, mountain goat and mule deer migration corridors. Many trails throughout the area for backcountry recreation and hunting.

access.directions: This park is located approximately 60 kilometres northwest of Lillooet.

rules.pets: Backcountry areas are rarely suited for dogs due to wildlife issues and the potential for problems with bears. Pets and domestic animals must be on a leash at all times. You are responsible for the behavior of pets and domestic animals and must dispose of their excrement.

visitorDetails.overview: Yard Creek Park is located east of Sicamous, along the Trans Canada Highway. The landscape surrounding Yard Creek Park is part of the Interior wet-belt, characterized by cedar and hemlock forest with lush undergrowth. The park contains a variety of bird species including American dippers. These fascinating little birds dive into the icy waters of the creek and “fly” along under the water in search of insects. Watch for them on the rocks along the creek. Established as a Class “A” park on March 16, 1956, for the purpose of providing a campground for the travelling public on the Trans-Canada Highway. As an outcome of the Okanagan Shuswap Land and Resource Management Plan, another 116 hectares were added to the park in 2004 under the Protected Areas of British Columbia Act, adding a strong conservation component to the park’s role.

activities.name: Hiking
activities.details: Yard Creek Park offers an extensive network of nature trails (Eagle River Nature Trails) on the North side of Highway 1. The trial head is accessible from the parking lot located at the west end of the park. Trail Map [PDF]

access.directions: This park is located approximately 15 kilometres east of Sicamous, along the Trans Canada Highway.

operations.notes:
Notes: Fires, wood cutting and vehicles are not permitted on the Nature Trails and can lead to fines under the Park Act . The Yard Creek campground is managed by the Yard Creek Park Caretaker (Columbia Shuswap Regional District). For more information: The Columbia Shuswap Regional District’s webpage .
A park gate is listed for this park; opening times and dates vary.

access.directions: Aylard Farm via Colwood exit, Sooke Road, Gillespie Road, East Sooke Road, Becher Bay Road. Anderson Cove via Gillespie Road then East Sooke Road. Pike Road via East Sooke Road and left Pike Road. About 1 hour from Victoria.
access.transportNotes: BC Transit 64 from 17 Mile House to stop near Anderson Cove; weekdays only, no weekend service. No transit to Aylard Farm or Pike Road.

visitorDetails.overview: Conjoined lakes with four beaches, picnic grounds, 15 km of walking trails including a 10 km loop, group picnic areas, seasonal Nature Centre, and accessible fishing dock. Elk Lake is stocked with rainbow trout. Some trails are multi-use; others hiking only.

access.directions: Beaver Lake: Pat Bay Highway to Royal Oak Drive then Elk Lake Drive. Filter Beds: Beaver Lake Road, 1.2 km from West Saanich Road or 800 m from Elk Lake Drive. Elk Lake: Sayward Road, Hamsterly Road, Brookleigh Road. About 20 minutes from Victoria.
access.transportNotes: BC Transit 70 or 72 to Elk Lake Drive at Beaver Lake entrance. For Elk Lake take route 70 or 72 to Pat Bay Highway at Sayward Road, then short walk.

trails.name: Named trails and routes
trails.description: 10 km loop. Filter Beds route is 5 km one way on smooth gravel with gentle slopes. Lakeside Trail follows the east lake shore on narrower natural surface.

rules.pets: Dogs controlled or leashed. Dogs excluded from designated beach or picnic areas at Beaver, Hamsterly, Eagle, and Water Ski beaches June 1 to September 15, except to pass through on leash without stopping. Hikers and cyclists yield to horses; leash dogs immediately near horses.
rules.cycling: Bicycles permitted on western part of 10 km Trail; some trails are multi-use, others hiking only. Motorized vehicles prohibited.

other.name: Park use
other.details: Boats limited to 10 horsepower, except higher horsepower in buoy-marked area. Stay on marked trails; no smoking, camping, open fires, or alcohol.

accessibility.summary: Hamsterly Beach has three accessible stalls, level packed-gravel paths, accessible toilet stalls, picnic tables, drinking fountain, and a Mobi Mat on the sandy beach. Main lake fishing pier is an accessible floating dock reached by low-slope ramps, with accessible stalls, toilets, picnic table, benches, and rod holders. Beaver Beach has accessible stalls, toilets, and routes to the 10 km trail and beach area. Filter Beds paths connect parking to accessible washrooms, picnic shelter, and trail.

visitorDetails.overview: A 205-hectare river corridor acquired by the RDN and conservation partners in 2005. It provides important salmon habitat, including a 4 km DFO side channel and a community hatchery, and supports wildlife such as elk, bears and cougars.

access.directions: Gravel parking is at the end of Allsbrook Road (drive through the yellow gate) and at the end of Chattell Road. From Chattell Road, walk across the suspension bridge to access the park.

operations.notes: The Allsbrook Road gate is open 7 am to 11 pm March 2 through October 31 and 7 am to 7 pm November 1 through March 1. Vehicles left after closing are locked in until 7 am.

Elsie King Trail is an 800 m self-guided loop of boardwalk and smooth gravel with signs, benches, shelter, and accessible toilet; boardwalk can be slippery when wet.

access.directions: Helmcken Road exit, Burnside Road West, Prospect Lake Road, then Munn Road. About 20 minutes from Victoria.

trails.name: Named trails and routes

access.directions: From Otter Bay ferry terminal take MacKinnon Road, Otter Bay Road, left Port Washington Road, right Bridges Road, then Upper Terrace Road. Alternate access is Ogden Road.

access.directions: From Victoria follow Fairfield Road, becoming Beach Drive in Oak Bay, then right on Denison Road. About 10 minutes from downtown.

scope.matchedName: Hamilton Marsh Regional Park and Conservation Area

visitorDetails.overview: A 364-hectare forest and wetland conservation area in the French Creek watershed, including a 36-hectare marsh. The site supports waterfowl, wildlife and species of conservation concern; easy walking trails and birdwatching are described.

access.directions: 505 Hilliers Road South. The site lies south of Qualicum Beach, bounded by Hilliers Road to the north and west, Memorial Avenue to the east, and the Island Corridor Foundation rail corridor to the south.

visitorDetails.overview: A 105-hectare park and campground below Mount Mark, beside Horne Lake. The park offers lake recreation and programmed activities; Horne Lake Caves Provincial Park is adjacent.

access.directions: 3890 Horne Lake Caves Road, Qualicum Beach.
access.address: 3890 Horne Lake Caves Rd, Qualicum Beach

rules.pets: Pets must be leashed and under control, including at individual campsites.

other.name: Smoking
other.details: Smoking is not permitted in the park, including at individual campsites.

other.name: Boat launch
other.details: Boaters must launch and remove vessels at the designated boat launch.

camping.summary: The park includes a campground beside the lake.

visitorDetails.overview: A 36-hectare park at north Saanich Peninsula. Summit Trail climbs a glacially rounded monadnock with views of Satellite Channel, peninsula, Gulf Islands, and San Juan Islands. Native plants, mushrooms, and spring wildflowers.

access.directions: Pat Bay Highway to Wain Road, west across highway, then right Tatlow Road. About 35 minutes from Victoria.

rules.pets: Dogs controlled or leashed. Hikers and cyclists yield to horses; leash dogs immediately near horses.
rules.cycling: Bicycles and motorized vehicles are not allowed.

other.name: Park use
other.details: Stay on marked trails and do not disturb plants or animals. Clean up after dogs and take trash away. Smoking, camping, open fires, and alcohol are not allowed.

operations.hours: Sunrise to sunset

visitorDetails.overview: Eastern Saanich Peninsula park with sandy beach, beach, dune, wetland and shrub ecosystems, migratory and resident birds, and fragile plants. A circular route follows the beach, foredune and inland trails past old salt marsh and back dunes.

access.directions: From Victoria take Pat Bay Highway, right Island View Road, then left Homathko Road to entrance. About 30 minutes; park is 12 km from Victoria Airport, 17 km from Swartz Bay terminal, and 20 km from downtown Victoria.

trails.name: Named trails and routes
trails.description: Beach-front accessible trail is about 1 km, wide packed gravel, with benches and campground connection.

maps.title: Island View Beach Regional Park map

rules.pets: Keep dogs controlled or leashed.
rules.cycling: Bicycles and motorized vehicles are not allowed.

other.name: Park use
other.details: Stay on marked trails and do not disturb plants or animals. Clean up after dogs and take trash away. Smoking, camping, open fires, and alcohol are not allowed.

accessibility.summary: No designated accessible campsites. Eight accessible parking stalls. Level packed gravel paths connect parking, picnic area, pit toilets, and beach-front trail. Main shelter and some tables have accessible overhangs. Seasonal mobility mat gives beach access.

operations.hours: Sunrise to sunset
operations.seasons: Campground operates Victoria Day long weekend in May through Thanksgiving long weekend in October. Seasonal beach mobility mat usually May to October as conditions permit.

camping.summary: Campground has 18 beachfront RV sites, 5 treed tent-trailer sites, 24 treed tent sites, all self-contained; garbage bins, pit toilets, drinking water, picnic areas, and group fire ring when no ban. All sites require advance online reservation, no first-come sites; 14-day annual maximum; bookings up to 30 days ahead. Fees omitted as volatile.

visitorDetails.overview: A 187-hectare coastal forest park on Juan de Fuca Strait. A short forest walk and stairs lead to Sandcut Beach, a long cobblestone shore with Olympic Peninsula views.

access.directions: From Victoria take Sooke exit and Highway 14 toward Jordan River about 55 km; Sandcut Beach parking is about 4 km east of townsite. About 1.5 hours.

rules.pets: Keep dogs controlled or leashed.
rules.cycling: Bicycles and motorized vehicles are not allowed.

other.name: Park use
other.details: Stay on marked trails; do not disturb plants or animals. Camping outside the campground, fires outside designated fire pits, smoking, and alcohol are not allowed.

operations.hours: Sunrise to sunset
operations.seasons: Campground operates year-round. Drinking water available April 1 to October 31.

camping.summary: Year-round campground has drive-in and walk-in self-contained sites, waterfront views, garbage bins, toilets, picnic areas, and fire rings when no fire ban. First come first served; no reservations. Maximum 14 days per calendar year. No hydro, dump station, or showers. Fees omitted as volatile.

visitorDetails.overview: Sooke River park at northwest end of Galloping Goose Trail, past Sooke Potholes. Old trails and roads cover almost 2 km of riverfront. Area adjoins historic Leechtown and has mining and railway logging remnants, including old equipment; named for lumberman Kapoor Singh Siddoo.

access.directions: No direct vehicle access. Reach by bicycle on Galloping Goose Trail or on foot from Sooke Potholes, 7.3 km one way. Drive to Sooke Potholes via Millstream Road exit, Veterans Memorial Parkway, Sooke Road, and Sooke River Road.

rules.pets: Keep dogs controlled or leashed.
rules.cycling: Cycling access is via the Galloping Goose Regional Trail; motorized vehicles are not allowed.

other.name: Park use
other.details: Stay on marked trails and do not disturb plants or animals. Clean up after dogs and take trash away. Smoking, camping, open fires, and alcohol are not allowed.

operations.hours: Sunrise to sunset

visitorDetails.overview: A small, rustic campground at the outskirts of Winter Harbour, a remote hamlet reached by an active logging road from Port Hardy.

access.directions: Winter Harbour is about 1.5 hours from Port Hardy on an active logging road.
access.transportNotes: The source advises carrying vehicle chains, driving with lights on, yielding to logging trucks, and preparing for possible road closure during severe weather.

other.name: Leave No Trace
other.details: Visitors are asked to follow Leave No Trace practices.

other.name: Hunting remains
other.details: Field dress animals where they are dispatched, not in or near the campsite, and contain remains in airtight sealed containers.

operations.notes: Remote community with limited services; fuel at the dock may be available but can change.

camping.summary: Eight sites with outhouses, fire pits and picnic tables. No water, sewer or electrical services. The site is rustic and the source says it is not suitable for tenting.
camping.reservationNotes: First come, first served. Limit stays to 14 days. Leave No Trace is requested.

contacts.name: Regional District of Mount Waddington Parks and Recreation

visitorDetails.overview: A small regional park with limestone and rock arch formations. A short woodland trail from the parking lot leads to a platform overlooking a rock bridge and pools, with further trails to cave formations, limestone arches and rock platforms.

access.directions: About a 20-minute drive from the Island Highway, according to the tourism listing.

operations.seasons: The tourism listing marks all four seasons.

background.conservation: The park offers an example of limestone features of the Quatsino Formation, which extends through much of northern Vancouver Island.

scope.matchedName: Little Qualicum River Estuary Regional Conservation Area

visitorDetails.overview: A 4.6-hectare sand spit at the mouth of the Little Qualicum River, west of Qualicum Beach, with critical marine and waterfowl habitat. Public access to the spit is restricted for conservation; the wildlife management area is generally accessible.

access.transportNotes: Public access to the spit itself is restricted; the wildlife management area is generally accessible.

visitorDetails.overview: A 111-hectare park on both sides of the Little Qualicum River, immediately downstream from Little Qualicum Falls Provincial Park. Rough trails reach the river; a developed trail from Meadowood Way links to the provincial park.

access.directions: 1240 Corcan Road, Qualicum Beach.

maps.title: Little Qualicum River Regional Park map

visitorDetails.overview: Park with rocky hillside vegetation and a 364 m summit overlooking the Malahat, Highlands, Victoria, and Olympic Mountains. Named for a four-metre Douglas-fir heritage tree that grew on the hillside for over two centuries. Spring wildflowers and raptors can be seen.

access.directions: From Victoria take Millstream Road exit, right on Millstream Road, left at Millstream Lake Road junction to continue on Millstream Road; entrance on right. About 30 minutes.

maps.title: Lone Tree Hill Regional Park map

rules.pets: Keep dogs controlled or leashed.
rules.cycling: Bicycles and motorized vehicles are not allowed.

other.name: Park use
other.details: Stay on marked trails and do not disturb plants or animals. Clean up after dogs and take trash away. Smoking, camping, open fires, and alcohol are not allowed.

operations.hours: Sunrise to sunset

visitorDetails.overview: A 156.97-hectare park with lake, sensitive ecosystems, sandy beach, and loop trail. Adjoins Roche Cove and Galloping Goose Trail. Swimming, picnicking, canoeing, fishing, hiking, and cycling access are described.

access.directions: Colwood exit, Old Island Highway/Sooke Road, Happy Valley Road, Rocky Point Road, then Matheson Lake Park Road. About 35 minutes.

rules.pets: Dogs controlled or leashed. Dogs excluded from designated main beach June 1 to September 15, except to pass through on leash without stopping. Hikers and cyclists yield to horses; leash dogs immediately near horses.
rules.cycling: Bicycles and motorized vehicles are not allowed.

other.name: Park use
other.details: Stay on marked trails and do not disturb plants or animals. Clean up after dogs and take trash away. Smoking, camping, open fires, and alcohol are not allowed.

operations.hours: Sunrise to sunset

visitorDetails.overview: A 25-hectare Galiano Island park with ocean-side bluffs, Active Pass views, and sensitive ecosystems. Ridge Trail is a 1 km crescent between points on Bluff Road; a separate hiking-only trail connects west to Bluffs Park.

access.directions: From Sturdies Bay Ferry Terminal follow Sturdies Bay Road 550 m, left Burrill Road, after 1.7 km continue Bluff Road 650 m, turn left and continue 500 m.

rules.pets: Keep dogs controlled or leashed.
rules.cycling: Bicycles and motorized vehicles are not allowed.

other.name: Park use
other.details: Stay on marked trails and do not disturb plants or animals. Clean up after dogs and take trash away. Smoking, camping, open fires, and alcohol are not allowed.

operations.hours: Sunrise to sunset

visitorDetails.overview: Salt Spring Island park named for remnants of an early 20th-century mill; a waterwheel remains. Has Saanich Inlet and Cowichan Bay views, old-growth forest, and rare plant habitat including Phantom Orchid. No public facilities or amenities.

rules.pets: Keep dogs controlled or leashed.
rules.cycling: Cycling only on designated trails; motorized vehicles are not allowed.

other.name: Park use
other.details: Stay on marked trails and do not disturb plants or animals. Clean up after dogs and take trash away. Smoking, camping, open fires, and alcohol are not allowed.

operations.hours: Sunrise to sunset

visitorDetails.overview: A 71.33-hectare park with Douglas-fir forest, Garry oak ecosystem, rocky 203 m summit, and views of Esquimalt Harbour and Victoria. Eastern trail connects across Trans-Canada Highway to Thetis Lake.

access.directions: Trans-Canada Highway exit 14 south, left Hoffman Avenue, right Winster Road, left Atkins Avenue to entrance. About 25 minutes.
access.transportNotes: BC Transit 50 to Western Exchange, then transfer to 53; stop near entrance.

rules.pets: Keep dogs controlled or leashed.
rules.cycling: Bicycles and motorized vehicles are not allowed.

other.name: Park use
other.details: Stay on marked trails and do not disturb plants or animals. Clean up after dogs and take trash away. Smoking, camping, open fires, and alcohol are not allowed.

operations.hours: Sunrise to sunset

visitorDetails.overview: A 35-hectare oceanfront conservation park on the former Camp Moorecroft site. A conservation covenant prioritizes ecological protection and enhancement while allowing low-impact recreation; habitats include Garry oak meadows and coastal Douglas-fir maritime ecosystems.

access.directions: 1563 Stewart Road, Nanoose Bay.

operations.notes: Park gates open 7 am to 11 pm March 2 through October 31 and 7 am to 7 pm November 1 through March 1. Vehicles left after closing are locked in until 7 am.

visitorDetails.overview: A park of more than 1,300 hectares including Mount Arrowsmith and Mount Cokely. Alpine meadows flower in late spring and early summer; high ridges support white-tailed ptarmigan. Long-standing alpine trails serve intermediate and experienced hikers.

access.directions: Recreational access uses private logging roads. Check Mosaic Forest Management's public access locations map for the Cameron Main Connector gate status; once on the logging road, stay left. Another access route climbs the Arrowsmith CPR Regional Trail and continues through ACRD Mount Arrowsmith Regional Park. The RDN warns this is a long, difficult hike taking at least 12 to 14 hours.
access.transportNotes: Private logging road access can change; check gate status before travel.

trails.name: Mount Arrowsmith alpine trails
trails.description: A network of long-standing alpine trails for intermediate and experienced hikers.

operations.seasons: Late spring and early summer are described as the alpine wildflower season.

visitorDetails.overview: An ACRD park on Mount Arrowsmith, about 20 km from Highway 4 by gravel logging road. Public trail access includes the Rousseau and Arrowsmith trails from Cameron Lake and the Lower Ski Area Trail.

access.directions: About 20 km from Highway 4 along a gravel logging road. Public access via the Rousseau Trail and Arrowsmith Trail from Cameron Lake and the Lower Ski Area Trail.
access.transportNotes: The access road crosses private forest lands and is an active logging road. The source says recreational access to Mosaic lands is available on weekends only in designated locations and advises checking current access openings.

operations.notes: Check Mosaic Forest Management access openings before departure.

visitorDetails.overview: A 292-hectare forested park on Mount Benson's upper northeast slopes, with panoramic views from Nanaimo to the Strait of Georgia. The Benson View Regional Trail climbs from the parking lot to the regional park and is steep and rough in places.

access.directions: 2761 Benson View Road, Nanaimo.

trails.name: Benson View Regional Trail
trails.description: Steep and rough in places. Allow three to five hours for a return trip and prepare for changing weather.

maps.title: Mount Benson Regional Park and Benson View Regional Trail map

operations.notes: Park gates open 5 am to 11 pm March 2 through October 31 and 5 am to 8 pm November 1 through March 1. Vehicles left after closing are locked in until 5 am.

visitorDetails.overview: Mount Cain is a ski area on Vancouver Island. The operator posts weekly updates about getting to, staying at and skiing the area. The operator's site recognizes Mount Cain as being in Namgis First Nation territory.

access.directions: From Highway 19, follow the Mount Cain signs onto a 16 km gravel access road. From the south, the turnoff is about 6 km north of the Highway 19 sign for Woss; from the north, it is about 8 km south of the Woss turnoff.
access.transportNotes: The operator requires vehicle chains that fit and can be used; chains may be needed in either direction and vehicles without chains may be denied access. The operator also advises bringing a shovel and checking local road and weather conditions.

rules.pets: Dogs must be leashed at all times.

other.name: Waste
other.details: Pack out all garbage, including compostable waste.

operations.notes: The operator provides weekly updates and posts road conditions as needed.

camping.summary: Parking-lot camping is allowed in the Main Parking Lot between its entrance and the L1 lift building.
camping.reservationNotes: Keep awnings, tarps and cooking areas behind vehicles; trailers are discouraged. Mid-week campers should use the uphill side of the lot. Generators must be off by 10 pm and quiet time starts at 11 pm.

background.culturalContext: The operator states Mount Cain is in Namgis First Nation territory; the nearby mountainous area is called Papikałan in Kwak'wala, meaning 'place of marmots'.

visitorDetails.overview: Mayne Island woodland trail through western red cedar, red alder, sword ferns, and Oregon grape to a ridge with panoramic land and sea views. Ravens, eagles, turkey vultures, and spring wildflowers are noted.

access.directions: Ferry from Swartz Bay to Village Bay, Mayne Island; follow Village Bay Road, right Fernhill Road, then right Montrose Road to entrance.

rules.pets: Keep dogs controlled or leashed.
rules.cycling: Bicycles and motorized vehicles are not allowed.

other.name: Park use
other.details: Stay on marked trails and do not disturb plants or animals. Clean up after dogs and take trash away. Smoking, camping, open fires, and alcohol are not allowed.

operations.hours: Sunrise to sunset

visitorDetails.overview: A 121-hectare wilderness park with second-growth forest, fragile mossy rock outcrops, Garry oak ecosystems, spring wildflowers, and views of Juan de Fuca Strait, Victoria, Sooke Hills, and Sea to Sea. Steep challenging trail climbs to 352 m summit. Protects Greater Victoria Water Supply Area.

access.directions: Millstream/Sooke exit, Veterans Memorial Parkway, Langford Parkway, Westshore Parkway, Meridian Avenue, Irwin Road, Humpback Road. About 30 minutes.
access.transportNotes: BC Transit 50 to Langford Exchange, transfer to 58 to Sooke Lake Road at Humpback Road; about 1.5 km walk.

rules.pets: Keep dogs controlled or leashed.
rules.cycling: Bicycles and motorized vehicles are not allowed.

other.name: Park use
other.details: Stay on marked trails and do not disturb plants or animals. Clean up after dogs and take trash away. Smoking, camping, open fires, and alcohol are not allowed.

operations.hours: Sunrise to sunset

visitorDetails.overview: A 743-hectare park with Killarney, Durrance, and Pease freshwater lakes. Durrance and Pease are described for canoeing and fishing; Durrance is stocked with rainbow trout and has accessible fishing dock. Summit Trail crosses glacial rock formations. Separate Mount Work-Hartland area has multi-use mountain bike trails.

access.directions: Main: West Saanich Road, Wallace Drive, Willis Point Road, Ross-Durrance Road. Durrance Lake: Durrance Close. Hartland: Hartland Avenue. Munn Road: Highway 1 exit 14, Millstream Lake Road, Munn Road. About 40 minutes.
access.transportNotes: Bus only to Hartland entrance: BC Transit 83 from Royal Oak Exchange to West Saanich Road at Hartland Road.

trails.name: Named trails and routes
trails.description: Summit Trail runs north-south across the park. Accessible Munn Road Loop is 630 m, smooth gravel, gentle slopes. Durrance Lake has a path leading to a narrow twisting hiking trail around the lake.

rules.pets: Keep dogs controlled or leashed.
rules.cycling: Mountain biking is allowed in the separate Mount Work-Hartland multi-use trail area; motorized vehicles are not allowed.

other.name: Park use
other.details: Stay on marked trails and do not disturb plants or animals. Clean up after dogs and take trash away. Smoking, camping, open fires, and alcohol are not allowed.

operations.hours: Sunrise to sunset

visitorDetails.overview: A 19.86-hectare park with second-growth Coastal Douglas-fir forest, Garry oak meadow, rocky outcrops, and arbutus. Supports Western Screech Owl and Common Nighthawk and forms part of Colquitz River headwaters via Excelsior Creek. Few simple trails; no public facilities or amenities.

rules.pets: Keep dogs controlled or leashed.

other.name: Park use
other.details: Stay on marked trails and do not disturb plants or animals. Clean up after dogs and take trash away. Smoking, camping, open fires, and alcohol are not allowed.

operations.hours: Sunrise to sunset

visitorDetails.overview: A 56-hectare conservation property protecting one of the few remaining natural forests along the lower Nanaimo River. Trails cross a mature Coastal Douglas-fir ecosystem; river access supports swimming, and the southeast area is dedicated to wildlife habitat.

access.directions: 1955 Frey Road, Nanaimo.

visitorDetails.overview: A 44-hectare oceanfront park in Crofton with calm water, pebble beaches, open fields and nature trails. It provides shoreline access and year-round off-leash dog use.

access.directions: Smith Road, Crofton. From Duncan, follow Herd Road to Osborne Bay Road, then Adelaide Street to Smith Road. From Nanaimo, use Chemainus Road, Crofton Road, Chaplin Road, York Street and Adelaide Street to Smith Road.

rules.pets: Off-leash dogs are welcome year round.

operations.hours: From dawn to dusk.

background.history: The park occupies former Morton and Gallagher family farmland. The CVRD acquired the property in 1979 through a land-gifting arrangement; management transferred fully to the CVRD in 2021.

visitorDetails.overview: Hardy Falls is a 6 ha shaded park at the south end of Peachland. A short, flat trail with multiple bridges over Deep Creek reaches a viewing platform at the falls. The park is noted for wildlife viewing, especially Kokanee salmon returning to spawn in fall.

access.directions: The parking lot is off Hardy Street in Peachland.

rules.pets: Dogs are allowed on leash.

operations.hours: Park hours shift seasonally: Jan 1-Feb 28, 6 a.m.-6 p.m.; Mar 1-May 31, 6 a.m.-9 p.m.; Jun 1-Aug 31, 6 a.m.-11 p.m.; Sep 1-Oct 14, 6 a.m.-9 p.m.; Oct 15-Dec 31, 6 a.m.-6 p.m.

visitorDetails.overview: Kalamoir is a 27.6 ha park on Okanagan Lake in West Kelowna, with beaches, a swimming platform, off-leash dog beaches, an accessible dock for launching canoes and kayaks, and trails of varying difficulty.

facilities.name: Accessible waterfront trail, dock and kayak launch

access.directions: The parking lot is at the end of Collens Hill Road. Access with limited street parking is also available at the ends of Sunnyside Road and Benedick Road near Casa Loma.

rules.pets: Dogs are allowed on leash in the park, with designated off-leash beaches.

operations.hours: Park hours shift seasonally: Jan 1-Feb 28, 6 a.m.-6 p.m.; Mar 1-May 31, 6 a.m.-9 p.m.; Jun 1-Aug 31, 6 a.m.-11 p.m.; Sep 1-Oct 14, 6 a.m.-9 p.m.; Oct 15-Dec 31, 6 a.m.-6 p.m.

visitorDetails.overview: Rose Valley is a 250 ha park in the Rose Valley neighbourhood of West Kelowna, with natural multi-use trails, valley views, a conservation area and natural pond where birds and other wildlife may be seen. Bodies of water are not managed by Regional Park Services.

access.directions: Parking is off Westlake Road near the pond and Rose Valley Elementary School, and off Westlake Road at Starlight Crescent.

rules.pets: Dogs are allowed on leash.

operations.hours: Park hours shift seasonally: Jan 1-Feb 28, 6 a.m.-6 p.m.; Mar 1-May 31, 6 a.m.-9 p.m.; Jun 1-Aug 31, 6 a.m.-11 p.m.; Sep 1-Oct 14, 6 a.m.-9 p.m.; Oct 15-Dec 31, 6 a.m.-6 p.m.

visitorDetails.overview: Raymer Bay is a 6.8 ha beach off Westside Road in West Kelowna, popular in summer for swimming and relaxing. It has mooring buoys, a playground and picnic shelter available for bookings.

access.directions: The parking lot is off Westside Road.

rules.pets: Dogs are not allowed.

operations.hours: Park hours shift seasonally: Jan 1-Feb 28, 6 a.m.-6 p.m.; Mar 1-May 31, 6 a.m.-9 p.m.; Jun 1-Aug 31, 6 a.m.-11 p.m.; Sep 1-Oct 14, 6 a.m.-9 p.m.; Oct 15-Dec 31, 6 a.m.-6 p.m.

visitorDetails.overview: Traders Cove is a 13.5 ha lakeshore park on Westside Road in West Kelowna, with two swim areas, mooring buoys, a playground and picnic shelter available for bookings.

access.directions: The parking lot is off Westside Road by the waste transfer station.

rules.pets: Dogs are allowed on leash in the upper section only.

operations.hours: Park hours shift seasonally: Jan 1-Feb 28, 6 a.m.-6 p.m.; Mar 1-May 31, 6 a.m.-9 p.m.; Jun 1-Aug 31, 6 a.m.-11 p.m.; Sep 1-Oct 14, 6 a.m.-9 p.m.; Oct 15-Dec 31, 6 a.m.-6 p.m.

visitorDetails.overview: Kopje is a 3.2 ha lakefront park in Lake Country with a playground, sports field, swimming areas and views of James Grant Island, a protected bird sanctuary. It contains the 1912 Gibson Heritage House. The fenced heritage house yard is available for wedding ceremony bookings.

access.directions: The parking lot is off Carrs Landing Road in Lake Country.

rules.pets: Dogs are generally not allowed. A seasonal program permits off-leash dogs from November 1 to March 31.

trails.name: Giscome Portage
trails.description: Historic overland route used by Lheidli T'enneh as a trade and harvesting route, and later by north- and south-bound travellers.

visitorDetails.overview: A 26-hectare Mayne Island waterfront park with forest, coastal areas, perimeter route, and two beaches. Easy paths reach beaches; a harder route follows rocky bluffs. Historically ŦÁ,WEN, a Coast Salish coho fishing site; area near entrance was farmed by Japanese settlers before World War II.

access.directions: Ferry from Swartz Bay or Tsawwassen to Village Bay, Mayne Island; follow Village Bay Road, right Fernhill Road, then right Horton Bay Road. Parking is limited to seven vehicles; roadside parking prohibited for emergency access.

visitorDetails.overview: A park in North Cowichan near Sansum Narrows, with views toward Salt Spring Island and a roughly 3.2 km loop trail starting and ending at the parking area.

access.directions: From the Trans-Canada Highway, take Trunk Road east, which becomes Tzouhalem Road. At the roundabout take Maple Bay Road, then turn right onto Genoa Bay Road. After the marina and Birds Eye Cove Farm, turn left onto Stoney Hill Road and continue about 1 km to the parking lot and trailhead.
access.address: Stoney Hill Regional Park, North Cowichan, BC, Canada

trails.name: Stoney Hill loop
trails.description: Scenic loop beginning and ending at the parking lot.

operations.hours: From dawn to dusk.

visitorDetails.overview: Large urban park with more than 40 km of recreation trails, lakes, beaches, Garry oak and Douglas-fir forest, swamp habitats, and 1958 nature-sanctuary designation. Upper and Lower Thetis Lakes support swimming, canoeing, and fishing; lakes stocked with catchable rainbow trout. Some blue-rated multi-use trails support cross-country mountain biking.

access.directions: Colwood exit from Trans-Canada Highway, follow Island Highway, right Six Mile Road. About 20 minutes from Victoria.
access.transportNotes: BC Transit 50 to Six Mile Road stop, then about 1 km walk.

rules.pets: Dogs controlled or leashed. Dogs excluded from designated Prior Lake beach/dock and Thetis Lake main beach or picnic areas June 1 to September 15, except to pass through on leash without stopping. Hikers and cyclists yield to horses; leash dogs immediately near horses.
rules.cycling: Mountain biking on designated trails. Only electric motorized boats on Thetis Lake; power boats prohibited on Prior Lake. Motorized vehicles prohibited.

other.name: Park use
other.details: Stay on designated trails. No camping, open fires, or alcohol. Swimming is unsupervised; cliff jumping is dangerous. Seasonal parking fees May 1 to September 30; amounts omitted as volatile.

accessibility.summary: Main Beach has accessible parking, low-slope routes, accessible washrooms, picnic tables, concrete pier, wide concrete ramp into water, and Mobi Mat. West Beach has accessible parking; trail surfaces vary.

operations.hours: Sunrise to sunset

visitorDetails.overview: Seashore park with woodland, Bilston Creek, salt marsh, sandy beach, and rocky headlands. Forest trail follows creek toward Sitting Lady Falls, trickle in summer and stronger cascade in winter. More than 160 bird species documented. Main entrance has 1.2 km moderate forest trail to beach.

access.directions: Main: View Royal/Colwood exit, Old Island Highway/Sooke Road, left Metchosin Road for 7 km. Tower Point: continue 5.8 km on Metchosin Road, left Duke Road, after 650 m right Olympic View Drive.
access.transportNotes: BC Transit 50 to Langford Exchange, transfer to 54 or 55 to Metchosin Road at Pears Road near main entrance.

trails.name: Named trails and routes
trails.description: Main entrance to beach: 1.2 km moderate forest trail, uneven and narrow, muddy after rain. Tower Point User-Friendly Trail: 500 m flat mixed gravel/dirt, can be muddy or slippery in rainy season.

rules.pets: Dogs controlled or leashed. Dogs excluded above natural sea boundary in beach areas except Tower Point June 1 to September 15, except to pass through on leash without stopping. Hikers and cyclists yield to horses; leash dogs immediately near horses.
rules.cycling: Bicycles and motorized vehicles are not allowed.

other.name: Park use
other.details: Stay on marked trails and do not disturb plants or animals. Clean up after dogs and take trash away. Smoking, camping, open fires, and alcohol are not allowed.

accessibility.summary: Tower Point user-friendly trail is 500 m, flat, mixed gravel and dirt.

operations.hours: Sunrise to sunset

visitorDetails.overview: A 15.5-hectare park beside Sooke Hills Wilderness Regional Park. Wrigglesworth Lake is the main attraction, reached by trail from Goldstream Heights Drive.

access.directions: Access from Goldstream Heights Drive; a trail leads from the road to Wrigglesworth Lake.
